newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour tackles Conservatives over tax.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour tackles Conservatives over tax.

text.p: Tony Blair's Labour Party opposition on Monday opened its last annual conference before an election by vowing to put tax and welfare reform at the heart of its campaign to end 17 years of Conservative rule.
Labour seized on disarray over tax cuts within the ruling party by reaffirming its goal to introduce a starting rate for income tax of just 10 to 15 percent, down from 24 percent now.

Economics spokesman Gordon Brown, contrasting his ambition with Conservative plans to scrap inheritance and capital gains taxes, said it was scandalous that high rates of tax made it not worthwhile for many unemployed people to look for a job.
"While the Tories (Conservatives) want a millionaires' tax cut for themselves, I want a peoples' tax cut for jobs... one that will help thousands back to work," Brown told delegates.
"This is a system designed to keep the unemployed poor and the poor unemployed. That is a gross injustice and under Labour the tax and benefit system... must be addressed," Brown said.

Brown was emboldened to take on the Conservatives on their favourite battleground, because of an admission by finance minister Kenneth Clarke that voters would not take any tax cuts in November's budget seriously unless they were justified.

Clarke's comments infuriated right-wing Conservatives, who are pinning their hopes on deep tax cuts to claw back Labour's commanding opinion poll lead of more than 20 percentage points in time for the election, due by May.
"Let the message go out: Kenneth Clarke now accepts the truth of what we have been saying for four years. You cannot trust the Tories on tax," Brown said.

In a speech that left no hostages to fortune in the way of tax commitments or new spending pledges, Brown warned delegates that a Labour government would need iron discipline on spending and faced no easy choices.

Labour is haunted by its candour at the last general election in 1992 when the Conservatives seized on its spending pledges to portray it as a party of crazed tax-raisers. Voters decided to play safe and re-elected Prime Minister John Major.

But Brown told left-wing traditionalists who would like to tax and spend more that Labour was not sacrificing its ideals. "Our prudence and responsibility is not therefore an abandonment of socialism; it is the very essence of it," Brown said.

The Labour leadership is keen to avoid open dissent at the conference from left-wingers. They are increasingly unhappy about Blair's reform of the party, which has moved it to the centre of British politics and away from its socialist roots.
The Left wants to hear more about how Labour cares for the poor and dispossessed rather than how their party will work in partnership with big business and attract middle-class voters.
The "people's tax cut" was the second eye-catching pledge of the opening day of the conference. Earlier, health spokesman Chris Smith vowed to end waiting lists for cancer surgery.

He said the promise, to be paid for by redirecting 100 million pounds ($156.1 million) a year from health service running costs, was a concrete example of how Labour would make a difference if it returned to power after 17 years in opposition.

Pledging to halt the encroaching privatisation of Britain's state-run health care system, Smith said: "Ask me why you should vote Labour. That reason will do alone. You will have a National Health Service again." ($1=.6408 Pound)
